newsitem.title: UGANDA: Ugandans dance, sing as Mrs Clinton visits.
newsitem.headline: Ugandans dance, sing as Mrs Clinton visits.

text.p: Ugandans danced and sang for U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton on Friday as she gave a morale boost to the country's work to fight AIDS, educate children and help women in small businesses.
Her visit, the first to Uganda by the wife of a sitting U.S. president, aroused much curiosity and thousands lined streets for a glimpse of Mrs Clinton and her daughter Chelsea, 17.

She was to speak to members of the Ugandan parliament, women, students and faculty from Makerere University before leaving later on Saturday for Eritrea, last stop on her two-week tour of six African countries.
At the dedication of Kampala's new AIDS information centre, Mrs Clinton was serenaded by young people living with infection.
"Get the facts and get to know what AIDS is all about," they sang. "Let's get together and fight until we reach the end."

About 500,000 Ugandans have died of AIDS and 1.5 million have it, but the centre's campaign is credited with helping contribute to a 50 percent reduction in new cases among young women, the greatest cut among all sub-Saharan countries struggling with the epidemic.
Janet Museveni, wife of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, gave a speech after the troupe sang in which she said Ugandans and other Africans used to abstain from sex before marriage.

"Now when we started adopting other people's behaviour, when we believed we were 'developing', when our society changed its way of life, when we had to send our young children to boarding schools where they stayed for longer periods of their lives without any parental guidance, all sorts of things started happening," she said.
Mrs Clinton praised President Museveni for having the "courage and openness" to confront the AIDS epidemic.

"It is not by chance that Uganda is the only country in Africa where so many people come voluntarily for HIV counselling and testing," she said. "We are beginning to win the battle against AIDS. We still have a very long way to go. But because of your efforts...we are making progress."
At Seguku Primary School, schoolchildren danced barefoot on the red clay ground to pounding drums. "You are welcome to Seguku, have a nice time," they sang.

The rural school outside Kampala benefits from U.S. aid and has nearly doubled its enrolment from last year after the government began a popular initiative to provide free primary education for four children in each family.
Mrs Clinton announced that Uganda's education system would receive a further $8 million in U.S. aid.
"There is nothing more important than investing in the education of boys and girls," she said.

She then went to nearby Bwaise Village to honour women who have taken advantage of a U.S.-backed scheme, the non-profit Federation for International Community Assistance, to obtain small loans to help build businesses.
Women have been able to get loans as small as $50 for such things as increasing the amount of food they can buy wholesale to sell in their shops.
The women danced and sang their praise for the programme.
"When women are given a chance to show their skills, to earn some income, they can do it very well," Mrs Clinton said.
